citations.desc: Consignments to carriers and intermediate handlers.
citations.narrative:
The registrant is not currently obtaining a certifying statement (e.g., “I hereby certify that the (number) primary
enclosure(s) which are used to transport the animal(s) in this shipment complies (comply) with USDA standards for
primary enclosures) from the consignor.
Not having a certifying statement such as the one above doesn't ensure that the animals being transported complies with
USDA standards for primary enclosures.
The registrant must start obtaining a certifying statement such as the one above from the consignors.
Correct starting on 6/13/26.

citations.desc: Primary enclosures used to transport live rabbits.
citations.narrative:
The registrant is not currently identifying the primary enclosures used to transport live rabbits with "Live Animal" signage
that is required in this this subsection and also does not have arrows or other markings to indicate the upright position of
the container.
Not having the required signage required in this subsection doesn't aide emergency professionals or individuals
responding to an emergency with the transport to be able to easily identify regulated animals that are being transported in
the vehicle.
Primary enclosures used to transport live rabbits, except where such primary enclosures are permanently affixed in the
animal cargo space of the primary conveyance, shall be clearly marked on top and on one or more sides with the words
“Live Animal” in letters not less than 2.5 centimeters (1 inch) in height, and with arrows or other markings, to indicate the
correct upright position of the container.
Correct starting on 6/13/26.

citations.desc: Primary conveyances (motor vehicle, rail, air, and marine).
citations.narrative:
On or about March 25th, 2026, the registrant had an in incident with her transport vehicle. The vehicle was in disrepair
and the registrant left for approximately 4.5-5 hours to pick up a part for the vehicle. During that time, the air conditioning
unit that was keeping the van cooled at 60 degrees Fahrenheit became unplugged. The temperature rose in the vehicle.
The registrant stated the outside temperature that day was 90 degrees Fahrenheit and she believes the temperature in
the van by the time she got back was also 90 degrees Fahrenheit. By the time the registrant came back, twenty rabbits
were deceased and ten rabbits were in physical distress. The registrant stated the live rabbits were panting and their
noses were wet.
Not keeping the temperature in the animal cargo space under 85 degrees Fahrenheit and not using ventilation, such as
fans, blowers, or air conditioners when the temperature exceeds 75 degrees Fahrenheit doesn't ensure the health and
well-being of the animals.
Auxiliary ventilation, such as fans, blowers, or air conditioners, shall be used in any cargo space containing live rabbits
when the ambient temperature in the animal cargo space is 75 degrees Fahrenheit or higher. The ambient temperature
within the animal cargo space shall not exceed 85 degrees Fahrenheit (29.5 °C).
Correct from this day forward (6/10/26).

On or about March 25th, 2026, the registrant had an in incident with her transport vehicle. The vehicle was in disrepair
and the registrant left for approximately 4.5-5 hours to pick up a part for the vehicle. During that time, the air conditioning
unit that was keeping the van cooled at 60 degrees Fahrenheit became unplugged. The temperature rose in the vehicle.
By the time the registrant came back, ten of the rabbits were in physical distress. The registrant stated the rabbits were
panting and their noses were wet. The registrant immediately provided care to the rabbits. She monitored and misted
them every 10 minutes for the next few hours. The rabbits recovered, but the registrant at no point contacted a
veterinarian.
Not visually observing all rabbits every 4 hours and not contacting a veterinarian when they become distressed doesn't
ensure the rabbits are receiving the optimal care while in transport.
All rabbits must be visually observed every 4 hours and a veterinarian must be contacted anytime a rabbit is showing
signs of obvious physical distress.
Correct from this day forward (6/10/26).
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the registrant.
End of report.
